etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English rehersen, from Anglo-Norman reherser (“to repeat word-for-word”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To repeat, as what has been already said; to tell over again; to recite.
(transitive) To narrate; to relate; to tell; to recount.
(transitive, intransitive) To practise by recitation or repetition in private for experiment and improvement, prior to a public representation, especially in theater.

quote.citation: 1648, Robert Herrick, “When he would have his verses read”, in Hesperides:
quote.text: In sober mornings, do not thou reherse / The holy incantation of a verse ...

quote.citation: 1736 March 16 (first performance; Gregorian calendar), Henry Fielding, Pasquin. A Dramatick Satire on the Times: […], London:  […]  J. Watts […], published 1736, →OCLC, Act I, page 1:
quote.text: I ſuppoſe vve ſhall hardly Rehearſe the Comedy this Morning; for the Author vvas Arreſted as he vvas going home from King's Coffee-houſe; and, as I heard, it vvas for upvvards of Four Pound: I ſuppoſe he vvill hardly get Bail.

definitions.definition: (transitive, theater) To cause to rehearse; to instruct by rehearsal.

quote.citation: 1859, Charles Dickens, “Darkness”, in A Tale of Two Cities, London: Chapman and Hall, […], →OCLC, book III (The Track of a Storm), page 231:
quote.text: He  […]  has been rehearsed by Madame Defarge as to his having seen Her  […]

quote.citation: 1916 March 11, Charles E. Van Loan, “His Folks”, in Saturday Evening Post‎[1]:
quote.text: It was plain that he'd been rehearsed a lot, but he wasn't letter-perfect by any manner of means.

definitions.definition: To contrive and carefully prepare (a story, etc.) to offer consistency.
